headline: Peconic stays warm and stretched thin — porgies still thick around Shelter Island, fluke sliding to the edges
subhead: Bottom bite carries the bay through late August while bass wait for cooler nights, and scallop talk starts creeping into the shops.
body_markdown:
The Peconic is running its classic late-August program, and if you've fished this system for any length of time, you know exactly what that means: the bay warmed up faster than the Sound back in May, and now it's holding that warmth longer into the fall, same as it always does. Surface temps are sitting in that mid-70s range across Shelter Island Sound, Noyack Bay, and up into Southold Bay, which is warm enough that fluke have quit stacking up and started spreading out across the flats. That's not a crisis, it's just biology — warm, thinner water holds less oxygen near bottom, and fluke respond by scattering rather than piling into tight pods. The ones still feeding hard are doing it where a cooler bottom layer survives: the channel edges off Jessup Neck, the deeper cuts running into Threemile Harbor, and the drop-offs on either side of Plum Gut where the tide keeps things scrubbed and oxygenated.

The moon is building toward full on Friday, and that's the piece worth tracking closest right now. We flagged this a week ago — that bait would start pushing toward the bay mouths as the tides tightened up heading into September — and that's exactly the pattern setting up. Bigger swings mean stronger current at the pinch points: Plum Gut, the Gut off Orient Point, the reef off Cedar Beach, the mouth of Coecles Harbor. Bait gets squeezed through those funnels harder on a big moon tide, and everything from snapper blues to weakfish to the occasional early-season striper starts stacking behind the bait rather than chasing it across open water. If you're planning your week around one tide, plan it around the peak of this building moon rather than the dead middle of a weaker cycle.

Porgy fishing remains the most dependable thing going in the bay right now, and Shelter Island is still the address. The rockpiles off Cedar Point, the drop-off outside Coecles Harbor, and the mussel bottom along the Sound side of the island are holding solid numbers of porgies in the 12- to 14-inch class, with a few chunkier fish mixed in on the better drifts. Standard bottom rig, size 4 or 6 hooks, a piece of clam or squid strip, fished right on bottom in 15 to 25 feet — nothing fancy needed, just patience and a chum pot if the current allows it. Slack tide and the first hour of either the incoming or outgoing tend to produce the steadiest action; once the current really starts ripping through the Sound side, the porgies tuck tighter to structure and the bite gets more technical.

Fluke are there, but call it a working bite rather than an easy one. Drift the edges of the channel running between Robins Island and North Sea, or work the deeper water off the mouth of Sag Harbor, using a bucktail-and-Gulp combination — white or chartreuse 4-inch swimming mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail — dragged slow along bottom on the last of the ebb, when the current is still moving enough to keep the bait ticking bottom but not so hard that you're bouncing off structure. Fish are running a mix of keeper-sized 18- to 20-inch fish and shorts, so expect to cull through some smaller ones to find your dinner fish. The days of just anchoring anywhere on the flats and hammering fluke are behind us for the season — the fish that are left have moved to where the water still makes sense for them.

Weakfish are mixing into those same bait drifts in modest numbers, mostly in the deeper holes off Threemile Harbor and around the mouth of Northwest Creek, taking small white bucktails and swimming plugs worked slow near bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing tide. Nothing to build a trip around specifically, but worth a few casts if you're already fishing that structure for fluke.

Bluefish continue to be the bay's most reliable performer, especially the snapper blues that have taken over the docks and bulkheads in Greenport, Sag Harbor, and Three Mile Harbor. Kids with a bobber and a sliver of spearing are having a field day most evenings around the tide change. Cocktail-sized blues in the 2- to 4-pound range are mixing into the fluke drifts along the channel edges too, which means anyone throwing bucktails should expect the occasional bitten-off leader.

Striped bass remain the quiet story right now — this is the predictable late-August holding pattern rather than any real push, with most bass tucked into deeper, cooler pockets during daylight and only showing consistently after dark around structure like the Plum Gut rips and the deeper drop-offs off Orient Point. That's expected. The real fall staging typically doesn't kick in until nighttime temperatures start dropping in earnest, likely mid-September this year given how warm the bay has run. Worth working the night tide at Plum Gut with bucktails or swimming plugs if you're set up for it, but don't expect a daytime bite to materialize yet.

One more thing worth flagging for the calendar: bay scallop season opener chatter is starting to circulate around the docks, right on schedule for this time of year. Nothing official to report yet, but if you're a scalloper, start paying attention to the sheds and the tackle shops over the next couple of weeks — that conversation always picks up steam as September approaches.
